A common path is medical laboratory or pathology-technology education, histology assistant work, independent slide preparation, responsibility for special stains and quality control, then laboratory supervisor or lead pathology technician.

paragraphs: In the morning, receive and register specimens and verify requisitions. Around midday, run dehydration and embedding and adjust microtome thickness. In the afternoon, stain and coverslip slides and review difficult cases with pathologists. Before leaving, complete quality checks and archiving and prepare large specimens for the next day.

In one sentence: turn human tissue into diagnostic slides. Work includes receiving, fixing, embedding, sectioning, staining, coverslipping, and quality control. It combines hand and eye as the front line of pathology diagnosis.

No matter how capable machines become, technicians still decide which section needs recutting, which stain is off, and which specimen does not match. Their eyes monitor, hands correct, and accountability remains. People cannot be removed from slide preparation.
In one sentence: the future needs histology technicians with quality-control thinking, difficult-case capability, and digital readiness, not people who only run procedures.
